title: Throwing a matched pair of candleholders
subtitle: Two matching cylindrical candleholders thrown in smooth stoneware, cone 6, using calipers to keep dimensions consistent
excerpt: A pair of matching candleholders is one of the first truly satisfying repetition exercises on the wheel. Each piece is a short, thick-walled cylinder with a recessed socket sized to hold a standard taper candle. The challenge is not technical difficulty but consistency: both holders need to look as though they came from the same hand on the same day. Calipers and a measured rim guide are what make that possible.
sourceNotes: Candleholder cylinder throwing pattern derived from first principles. Matched-pair repetition throwing principles documented in Leach, A Potter's Book (1940). V&A open-access collection for turned candleholder forms.

content.text: A pair of thrown cylindrical candleholders is a classic beginner throwing project with a clear functional target: two pieces that match. Each holder is a short cylinder with a thickened base and a recessed
candle socket

at the top centre, sized to grip a standard 22 mm taper candle. The walls are deliberately thick for stability, which suits a beginner weight of clay and gives the pieces a solid presence on the table.

The skill at beginner level is keeping both pieces the same height and diameter. Calipers set to the target dimensions after throwing the first piece are the tool that makes the second match the first. Measure at every stage: rim diameter, height, and socket depth.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need

materials.name: Mid-fire glaze, pre-mixed
materials.quantity: enough to glaze both holders inside and out

content.text: Preparation

Divide 600 g of smooth stoneware into two equal 300 g balls. Weigh each ball on a kitchen scale: matching weights are the foundation of matching sizes. Wedge both balls thoroughly. Throw the first holder, measure it carefully with calipers once you are satisfied with its height and socket depth, and write those measurements down before throwing the second. A taper candle socket needs to be exactly 22 mm in internal diameter and at least 20 mm deep to grip reliably. Have the candle itself on the bench as a test gauge.
Throwing
Centre 300 g of stoneware on the bat. The lump should be tight and round, with no visible wobble, before you open it.
Open a floor 50 mm in diameter, leaving 10 to 12 mm of clay at the base. This is thicker than most thrown forms and gives the holder the stability it needs when the candle is burning.

Pull the walls upward in two passes to a height of 70 mm. Keep the walls thick: 8 to 9 mm throughout. The holder should feel weighty and solid. A narrow cylinder with thick walls is more stable than a thin-walled one at this height-to-diameter ratio.
At the final pass, collar the rim in slightly to close the cylinder to a rim diameter of 60 to 65 mm. Smooth the outside with a wooden rib held against the wall as the wheel turns slowly.
Create the
candle socket

: with the wheel stationary, press two fingers gently into the centre of the rim to open a small well 22 mm in diameter and 20 to 25 mm deep. The socket walls should be 6 mm thick. Smooth the inside of the socket with a small wet finger.

Test the socket with the taper candle: the base of the candle should enter the socket with light hand pressure and feel held, not loose. If the socket is too wide, pinch gently inward at the socket lip while the clay is still soft.

Smooth the rim with the chamois leather. Use the needle tool to level the rim if it is uneven: hold the needle at the target height against the inside rim wall as the wheel turns slowly, then lift off the clay above the cut.
Set the calipers to measure the rim diameter and the height of the finished piece. Record both numbers. Wire off and set aside on the bat to dry to
leather-hard
Throw the second holder immediately, using the recorded measurements to guide every stage. Check against the calipers after pulling and again after forming the socket.
Trimming
At
leather-hard
, invert each holder onto the wheel head and centre it. Coil a thin ring of clay around the rim to grip it in place.
Trim a
foot ring
5 mm tall and 5 mm wide using the loop tool, at a diameter of 40 mm. This gives a stable, neat base with the thick base wall still intact above it. Smooth the foot ring edges.

Check that both holders match in overall height when placed upright side by side on a flat surface. If one is visibly shorter, that is a lesson for the next pair rather than a problem to fix now: the height is set at the throwing stage.
Drying
Dry the trimmed holders slowly upright to
bone-dry

. Thick-walled forms dry more slowly than thin ones. Cover loosely for the first 24 hours, then uncover. The candle socket area may feel damp long after the outer wall has stiffened: check inside the socket before loading for bisque.
Bisque firing
Load both holders upright on the same kiln shelf so they fire at identical conditions.
Bisque
fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius) with a slow initial ramp: 60 degrees Celsius per hour to 120 degrees Celsius, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Hold for 10 minutes at peak.
Glazing and glaze firing

Glaze the exterior of each holder by dipping or brushing. A single-colour glaze on both is the most effective way to reinforce the matched appearance. Glaze inside the candle socket too: pour a small amount of glaze in, roll it around, and pour out. Leave the foot ring and base free of glaze. Clean all glaze from the foot ring and 5 mm of the base. Load both holders on the same shelf for the glaze firing at cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius). Firing them together at the same position in the kiln minimises colour variation between the pair.
Care

Fired stoneware candleholders are sturdy and heat-resistant to the temperatures produced by a burning taper candle. Never leave a burning candle unattended. If a candle burns down into the socket and wax accumulates, place the holder in the freezer for 30 minutes: the wax contracts and lifts out cleanly without damaging the glaze. Wipe with a dry cloth only; soap can leave a residue inside the socket.
Variations

A trio of three holders at staggered heights from a single batch makes a more dramatic table centrepiece than a pair. Make one at 70 mm, one at 90 mm, and one at 55 mm from the same 300 g ball adjusted by a 50 g increment. Keep the socket size identical in all three.

For pillar candles rather than tapers, open the socket to 65 mm in diameter and 10 mm deep instead: the pillar sits in a shallow recess rather than a gripping socket. The wall around the recess can be shaped into a shallow lip with the chamois leather for a more refined look.

rows.problem: Candle socket too wide after firing
rows.cause: Clay shrinks approximately 12 percent during drying and firing; a socket that fits the candle in the greenware stage will be too small after firing
rows.fix: Make the greenware socket approximately 25 mm in diameter, not 22 mm. Test with the actual candle after bisque firing before glaze firing.

rows.problem: Second holder shorter than the first
rows.cause: Second ball was pulled to a different height
rows.fix: Note the exact height measurement after the first pull and use the needle tool held at that height as a guide when pulling the second piece.

rows.cause: The socket area dried faster than the outer wall due to its smaller enclosed mass
rows.fix: After forming the socket, drape a small piece of plastic over the top of the holder during drying so the socket dries at the same rate as the rest of the piece.

rows.cause: Clay too dry at trimming stage
rows.fix: Trim at true leather-hard: the clay should feel cool to the touch and yield slightly under fingernail pressure without crumbling.
